reference.source: ATS/ERS classification of idiopathic interstitial pneumonias / Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
clinicalPearls: A subacute illness with cough, breathlessness, malaise, low-grade fever, and weight loss over weeks, often mistaken initially for a community-acquired pneumonia that fails to respond to antibiotics
The term cryptogenic denotes the idiopathic form; identical organising pneumonia can be secondary to infection, drugs, connective tissue disease, radiation, or aspiration
High-resolution CT typically shows patchy peripheral or peribronchial consolidation and ground-glass opacity that is frequently migratory over time
Suggestive CT signs include the reversed halo (atoll) sign and a perilobular pattern of consolidation
Histology shows intraluminal plugs of granulation tissue (Masson bodies) within distal airspaces and alveolar ducts, with preserved lung architecture
Response to corticosteroids is characteristically prompt and often dramatic, which supports the diagnosis
Relapse is common when steroids are tapered too quickly, so treatment is usually prolonged and reduced gradually
Always search for a secondary cause before labelling organising pneumonia as cryptogenic
reference.pathophysiology: Organising pneumonia is a stereotyped repair response of the distal lung to epithelial injury. Damage to the alveolar and bronchiolar epithelium allows leakage of plasma proteins and recruitment of fibroblasts that organise into buds of granulation tissue filling the alveolar ducts and alveoli (Masson bodies), sometimes extending into respiratory bronchioles. Because the underlying lung architecture and interstitial framework are preserved, the process is largely reversible and responds well to corticosteroids. When no trigger such as infection, drug, radiation, or connective tissue disease is identified, the disorder is termed cryptogenic organising pneumonia.
additionalDifferentials: Connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution CT to identify migratory peripheral/peribronchial consolidation, the reversed halo sign, and perilobular opacities
Bronchoalveolar lavage showing mixed cellularity, useful mainly to exclude infection, eosinophilia, and malignancy
Surgical or transbronchial (including cryobiopsy) lung biopsy demonstrating intraluminal granulation-tissue plugs
Connective tissue disease and vasculitis serology to detect a secondary cause
Review of drug history and prior radiotherapy as potential triggers
Pulmonary function tests, typically showing a restrictive defect with reduced gas transfer
redFlags: Rapidly progressive or fulminant respiratory failure suggesting an aggressive fibrosing variant
Failure to improve with corticosteroids, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
Features pointing to an underlying vasculitis, connective tissue disease, or malignancy
Frequent relapse on tapering requiring re-evaluation and treatment intensification
reference.prognosis: Most patients with cryptogenic organising pneumonia respond well and often completely to corticosteroids, although relapses during dose reduction are common; a minority have a progressive fibrosing course with a poorer outcome.
pitfalls: Persisting with repeated antibiotic courses for a 'pneumonia' that is actually organising pneumonia
Labelling the disease cryptogenic without excluding drug, infection, radiation, and connective tissue disease causes
Tapering corticosteroids too rapidly and precipitating relapse
Relying on non-specific bronchoalveolar lavage findings rather than correlating imaging and, when needed, histology
references: ATS/ERS international multidisciplinary classification of idiopathic interstitial pneumonias
Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
management: Systemic corticosteroids as first-line disease-specific therapy, typically producing a prompt clinical and radiological response
Prolonged, gradual corticosteroid taper because relapse commonly occurs during dose reduction
Add a steroid-sparing immunosuppressant such as azathioprine or mycophenolate, or a macrolide, in relapsing or corticosteroid-dependent disease
Exclude and treat any secondary trigger, reviewing drug and radiotherapy history and screening for infection or connective tissue disease
Supportive care with supplemental oxygen, smoking cessation and pulmonary rehabilitation as needed
Monitor with serial high-resolution CT and pulmonary function tests, with bone protection and glucose monitoring while on corticosteroids
Refer to a respiratory multidisciplinary team and escalate for a progressive fibrosing course or respiratory failure
